card.hook: Everyone queues up for the front of Palermo Cathedral, but the quiet back of it is where the fun is. Three curved walls covered in arches and zigzag patterns, and hardly anyone in your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Sett'Angeli, at the rear of the cathedral, and face the building so all three apses are in front of you. These are the oldest outside walls, from the original 12th-century church.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole back of the building. If the square is too tight for all three apses, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep the phone level so the edges don't stretch. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the arches and patterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the apses up with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean, then tap the stonework and slide it a touch darker so the pale sky doesn't wash out the detail.
card.best_time: Morning light is likely to suit the apses best, and it's quieter early too. Check the light on the day, as the high walls can throw shade across the square.
card.selfie_here: Go round to the front and use the flower-planted fountain in the open area in front of the cathedral's façade. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and hold it low, so the carved front and the fountain sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: In the rectangular square at the front, where the statues of bishops and saints stand, stand with the façade behind you and ask a passer-by to step back and frame you with the whole front in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Piazza Sett'Angeli is an open public square. Entry to the cathedral is free, but the roof, royal tombs and treasury need a ticket, and opening hours change with services, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fill the whole frame with nothing but arches and patterns, no sky at all, then step back and take one wide shot of all three apses to compare.
card.good_to_know: The first church on this site was Byzantine, and the present cathedral was begun in 1185 by Archbishop Walter Ophamil. The big dome and neoclassical look came later, from work done between 1781 and 1801. The patterns on the apses echo those at Monreale Cathedral.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Sett'Angeli, at the rear of the cathedral, and face the building so all three apses are in front of you. These are the oldest outside walls, from the original 12th-century church.

card.hook: Picture a flight of wide steps, a row of tall columns and a bronze lion standing guard on each side. That's Teatro Massimo, and it practically poses for your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Piazza Giuseppe Verdi, facing the front of the theatre, which lies to the south-east. Step back as far as the square allows so the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole facade and its columns in one frame. If the edges look stretched or the square is busy, switch to 1x and step back. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the bronze lions and the column tops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line a column or the central doorway up with the middle line, and keep your phone level so the columns don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: About 45 minutes before sunset is suggested for the front. Sunset changes with the season, so check the time on the day.
card.selfie_here: Head up to the terrace at the top of the steps, by the columns, and use the front camera with the theatre behind you and Piazza Verdi opening out in front. You can also try beside the bronze lion on the left of the stairs as you face the building.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the square on the north side while you pose on the steps, so the whole facade and its dome fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is usually not allowed inside the theatre, and photos are typically not allowed during performances. The marble staircase can be slippery, so wear comfy, non-slip shoes. The inside is open only on paid guided tours, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Get both bronze lions in one frame with a stranger walking past for scale, then see if your friends can spot the lions.
card.good_to_know: Teatro Massimo is the largest theatre in Italy. It opened on 16 May 1897 with Verdi's Falstaff, after building began in 1874 and paused for eight years. It closed for repairs in 1974 and stayed shut until 1997. Film fans may know it from the closing scenes of The Godfather Part III.

card.hook: Here's a twist: the best photo of the Capuchin Catacombs is the one you take before you walk in. Inside, the phone stays in your pocket, so the outside is your souvenir.
card.stand_here: Stand outside the Capuchin monastery at Piazza Cappuccini, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the building and step back a little so the whole frontage fits.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the entrance and the frontage. If you're close to the building and it won't all fit, tap 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building's vertical lines straight, then tap the building and drag the slider to make it a bit darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go in the daytime, when the light is clear and the entrance is easy to see. Earlier in the day is likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try outside the entrance on Piazza Cappuccini, where one visitor posed for a selfie with a Capuchin friar. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and keep the building over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography inside is officially prohibited, and signs and staff will tell you so, so keep your phone away once you go through the door. Access is by stairs only. One visitor suggests leaving your selfie stick at the hotel, though that's their advice, not an official rule.
card.challenge: Get one straight-on shot of the frontage with the gridlines lined up, and not a single stranger in it.
card.good_to_know: The monks began digging crypts here in the 16th century, when their old cemetery ran out of room. In 1599 they placed Brother Silvestro of Gubbio here, and local families later paid to have relatives preserved too. A 2011 census counted 1,252 mummies, among about 8,000 bodies. Opening times and entry rules can change, so check the official site before you go.

card.hook: Picture 8 AM at Ballarò: stallholders are still stacking fruit and veg into neat, bright displays, and you can frame a shot without a crowd in the way. By lunchtime it's a different show, so this is the quiet-colour version.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Via Porta Carini entrance to the market, with the Ballarò stalls on Via Ballarò about 900 m to the south-east. Face along the line of stalls and stay to the side so you don't block the way in or out.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for stalls and displays. Use zoom 0.5x in the narrow bits to fit a whole stall front, and zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for details or to photograph people from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the produce, then slide the picture a touch darker so the bright colours don't wash out, and switch on gridlines to keep the stall edges straight.
card.best_time: Around 8 AM, when vendors are arranging their produce. One guide says 8-9 AM, so treat that as approximate.
card.selfie_here: Try the corner where Via Ballarò meets Via del Bosco: use the front camera, zoom 0.5x, and put the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore over your shoulder with the busy stalls below it. For something more fun, take one at the Via Ballarò end by the fish stalls with the whole swordfish and tuna, which is less crowded than the Piazza del Carmine end.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the Via Porta Carini entrance, ideally around 8 AM, while you stand inside the market with the stalls stretching away behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Ask before photographing vendors or people up close; a smile and a gesture usually does it, and some vendors may ask for a small payment. Leave valuables behind, keep your bag zipped, and keep your phone in your hand or on a wrist strap, because pickpockets are described as rampant in this part of Palermo.
card.challenge: Find the neatest stack of fruit or veg and fill the whole frame with it, then see if you can beat it with a swordfish.
card.good_to_know: Ballarò is one of Palermo's busy street markets, and it works best as a scene of people and food rather than a single building. Its stalls run along Via Ballarò, with the dome of the Chiesa del Carmine Maggiore rising behind the crowd. Stalls change from day to day, so take what you see as a guide, not a promise.

card.hook: Most people walk straight into the middle of Quattro Canti and spin in circles. Start up the street instead, where Via Maqueda lines up like a runway and the square waits at the far end.
card.stand_here: Go to the top of the Teatro Massimo steps, facing Piazza Giuseppe Verdi, then look down Via Maqueda. The Quattro Canti is about 655 m to the south-east, at the far end of the street.
card.zoom: From the steps, try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the far end of the street closer. Down in the square, switch to 0.5x to fit all four facades in, or use 1x for one facade at a time.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the street edges up with them, so Via Maqueda leads the eye straight to the buildings.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or in the evening. Midday is busy, and people and traffic will wander through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand on one corner of the crossing (Piazza Vigliena) and face into a street, so one of the four baroque facades fills the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the crossroads while you stand on a corner, so the whole octagon of facades fits in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Cars and motorbikes sometimes pass through the square, even though this stretch is mostly pedestrian, so look around before you step back for a photo.
card.challenge: Take one straight-on shot of a single facade with the fountain, the statues and the roofline all in the frame, and see if you can do it without a scooter photobombing you.
card.good_to_know: Quattro Canti is officially called Piazza Vigliena, and it was laid out between 1608 and 1620 on the orders of the Spanish Viceroys. The square is an octagon: four sides are streets and four are matching curved facades, each four storeys high. Each facade has a seasonal fountain at the bottom, statues of Spanish rulers of Sicily above it, and statues of four female patron saints of Palermo at the top.

card.hook: Step inside and your neck gets a workout before your phone does: gold mosaics on every wall, and a honeycomb-style wooden ceiling above with painted musicians, hunters and animals. It's small, but you'll want to look slowly.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon in the Cappella Palatina, in the Norman Palace in Palermo. You're in the middle of the chapel, so face down the nave toward the three apses.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole nave and ceiling in one shot. Then go to 1x for the walls and arches, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out mosaic figures and ceiling details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap a bright patch of gold mosaic, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the gold stays rich instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go in the first hour after the chapel opens, when it's the quietest for photos. You'll get a cleaner view down the nave and room to stand still.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, head outside to the Villa Bonanno park and stand next to the stone statue of Philip V with the palace behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so the whole palace fits over your shoulder. The chapel is inside the palace, so this is the best palace-backed selfie spot rather than one with the chapel itself.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back on Piazza Indipendenza facing the palace front, while you stand in front of the palace so they can fit the whole façade in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the chapel. Photos without flash are generally fine, but check the official site for the current photography rules before you go.
card.challenge: Play 'spot the musician': find a painted musician, hunter or animal on the ceiling and catch it in a close-up at 5x without tilting your phone sideways.
card.good_to_know: King Roger II commissioned the chapel in 1132, building over an older chapel from around 1080 that is now the crypt. Its design mixes Byzantine, Norman and Fatimid styles. The ceiling is the earliest surviving wooden example of its kind, with about 75 inscriptions, and UNESCO recognised the site in 2015.

card.hook: Palazzo dei Normanni is so long that you'll probably find yourself shuffling backwards across the square, still not fitting it all in. Keep going, the square gives you room.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza del Parlamento, right in front of the main façade, and face the palace straight on. Stand back, hold your phone level, and leave a strip of empty square at the bottom of the picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole long façade in. Then go to 1x for a more natural look, and try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the pointed windows and the arcaded loggia.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the pale façade, then drag the slider to make it a touch darker, so the limestone keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Softer morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to pale stone than harsh midday sun. In the evening, head to Via del Bastione for the lit façade and the golden mosaics against the sky.
card.selfie_here: Try the square in front of the palace, with the façade behind you. One page lists Piazza della Vittoria as a square the palace front faces, but it isn't named as a best selfie spot, so treat it as a good guess. card.rules_and_safety: The palace is a working parliament building, so check the official site before you go for the interior, gardens and terraces. Some places inside, like the Cappella Palatina, may ban flash or all photography, so check on arrival. Wear comfortable shoes, because the chapel floors are slippery polished marble.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and find one run of arches. Can you get every line dead level, with no leaning walls?
card.good_to_know: It's often described as the oldest royal residence in Europe. The Normans built their palace here after the conquest of 1072, on the site of an earlier Arab-period fortress. Since 1946 it has housed the Sicilian Regional Assembly, and inside is the Cappella Palatina, famous for its mosaics and painted wooden roof.

card.hook: Picture 644 pieces of marble arriving in Palermo, and then you trying to squeeze the whole thing into one photo. The square gives you almost no room to step back, so you'll need a plan.
card.stand_here: Stand on the steps of Palazzo Pretorio, if you're allowed up there, and face across the fountain toward Via Maqueda. The fountain sits to the north-west of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole fountain in one frame. Then try 1x for a tidier view, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for faces, reliefs and niches.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight so the tiers don't lean, with the fountain in the lower half and the buildings behind it.
card.best_time: Early morning is quieter, and late afternoon gives a warmer glow. After dark the fountain is lit from below, so switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: If the barriers allow it, sit on the rim of the basin and use the front camera at 0.5x so you and the fountain both fit in. For another angle, stand on the Via Maqueda side in late afternoon and turn so the fountain is over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the town hall steps (Palazzo Pretorio) looking across toward Via Maqueda, while you pose near the fountain so they get the full composition.
card.rules_and_safety: The fountain has a fenced edge, so don't climb the statues, and the steps may be restricted, so only use them if allowed. Renovation work has been reported, and it's worth keeping an eye on your belongings in the busy parts of the piazza.
card.challenge: Hunt for one of the animals hiding among the gods and get a close-up of it, then take a second shot from low down to show how tall the fountain is.
card.good_to_know: The fountain was made in Florence in the sixteenth century by Francesco Camilliani. Palermo bought it, took it apart into 644 pieces, and rebuilt it in the square after it arrived on 26 May 1574, with Camillo Camilliani finishing the work in 1581. All those nude statues earned it the nickname "Piazza della Vergogna" (Square of Shame).

card.hook: Somewhere in Palermo, a fishmonger is cutting a fish on a trestle table in the open air while the seller next to him shouts about his produce. That's La Vucciria, and it's busy, a bit rough around the edges, and great for photos.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Caracciolo, at the south end where the market finishes. Face the fishmongers' trestle tables, with the produce and fabric stalls behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the scene as your eye sees it. Switch to 0.5x when the alleys feel too tight, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a fish table or stall from a polite distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put a fish table on one of the lower lines, with the stalls and people filling the top of the frame.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, roughly 8 to 10 a.m. The square is partly shaded then and the light is softer than at midday. Stall hours vary, so check locally before you set out.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Piazza Caracciolo, at the fish-cutting stalls, with the stalls and crates behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it, so more of the scene fits over your shoulder. You can also stand just inside the main entrance under the Vucciria sign, with the market lanes behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Piazza San Domenico, a few steps back from the entrance, while you stand just inside under the Vucciria sign, so they catch the sign and the lane in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: One visitor guide suggests leaving valuables at home and eating before you arrive, since the area is busy at night. Ask before taking close portraits of people.
card.challenge: Find a hand-painted sign and get it in the shot with a seller at work. Bonus points if nobody notices you taking it.
card.good_to_know: La Vucciria is one of Palermo's old market districts, in the Castellammare quarter. Its name is a puzzle: some say it comes from 'voce' (voice) for the noise of the sellers, others from the French 'boucherie' (butcher's shop). Just off Via Argenteria, in front of the ruined church of Sant'Eulalia dei Catalani, there's one of the oldest carved images of the Genius of Palermo in the city.

card.hook: Four bronze horses are charging across the top of a theatre, and nobody in the square seems to notice. Look up: that's Apollo and Euterpe riding the quadriga, a four-horse chariot group by Mario Rutelli.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Ruggero Settimo, in the middle of Palermo, and face the theatre head-on. Put the Ruggero Settimo monument in front of you, low in the picture, with the arch and the horses filling the top.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the classic straight-on view. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the monument, the whole front and some sky. Try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the horses and the arch.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the front straight, then tap the facade and slide it a little darker so the sky stays blue and the stonework doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: After dark is best, when the building is lit up and the square looks really striking. Daytime works too, but expect more people in the foreground.
card.selfie_here: Stand by the Ruggero Settimo monument with the theatre behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low, so the arch and the horses sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner of Via Emerico Amari and Via Ruggero Settimo and shoot across toward the theatre, while you stand near the monument so the whole front and its approach fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is an open public space. If you want to go inside or catch a performance, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the monument, the arch and all four horses in one frame, then take a second shot with the palm tree framing the side.
card.good_to_know: The theatre opened on 7 June 1874 with Bellini's I Capuleti e i Montecchi. It took the Garibaldi name after his death in 1882. Today it's the second most important theatre in the city after the Teatro Massimo, and the home of the Orchestra Sinfonica Siciliana.

card.hook: Picture a tree so big its roots hang down like curtains, and you're standing right under it. That's the fig in Piazza Marina's Garibaldi Garden, and it's the best reason to get your phone out here.
card.stand_here: Stand in Giardino Garibaldi, beneath the largest fig trees, around the turtle pond. Face the thick trunks and hanging roots, with the garden's greenery and the edge of the square behind them. The Fontana del Garraffo is to the west, about 2 minutes on foot.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the fig trunks and roots, so you can squeeze in the whole tangle. Switch to 1x for the square's façades and the fountain. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it for balconies and lamp posts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put one thick trunk on a vertical line, then crouch low and tilt the phone up so the roots hang through the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. At midday the tree shade helps. Skip Sundays if you can, because the flea market fills the square and you'll struggle to get a clear frame.
card.selfie_here: Try beneath the biggest ficus canopy near the turtle pond, where the giant tree can fill the frame behind you. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a little low so the tree sits over your shoulder. In the morning, the benches on the north side of the garden are a nice alternative, with the tree showing from root to crown behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says photography is generally allowed in Piazza Marina for personal use.
card.challenge: Find a root that hangs all the way down and make it the star: shoot it from low down, then take one more shot with a friend peeking out from behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Garibaldi Garden was designed by Giovan Battista Filippo Basile in 1863 and is known for the biggest Ficus macrophylla in Europe. In the Middle Ages this square was a swamp linked to the old port, the Cala, and it was cleared in the 14th century. In 1909 the New York police officer Joe Petrosino was killed here, and a small brass memorial plate on a pole recalls him.

card.hook: Palermo packs three centuries of styles into one little square, and you can catch the show without stepping inside. From Piazza Bellini, a Baroque facade and bell tower sit right beside the red domes of San Cataldo.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Bellini, across the square from the church facade, and face south-east. You'll see the Baroque facade and bell tower with San Cataldo's red domes beside them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the facade and the domes together. If the square is busy and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x. Then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the bell tower and the red domes.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the bell tower up with a vertical line so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the stonework and the square has fewer people. If you want to go inside, check the official site for visiting times.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the open square in front of the church's facade, with the church behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit more in, and hold your arm out so the church shows over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the centre of Piazza Bellini, facing the church, so the whole facade and bell tower fit in the frame, while you pose in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so modest dress is expected. Photos inside are generally fine, but skip the flash, especially during services, and look for signs as rules may differ.
card.challenge: Get both churches in one frame with the bell tower perfectly straight, then take a second shot of just the red domes.
card.good_to_know: The church is also called La Martorana. It was founded by George of Antioch, chief minister of King Roger II of Sicily, with a charter dated 1143, and was complete by his death in 1151. Nuns later altered it between the 16th and 18th centuries, and they were known for fruit-shaped marzipan, still sold in Palermo pastry shops. Since 2015 it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

card.hook: Rough stone below, pretty paired windows above, battlements on top: Palazzo Chiaramonte looks like a castle that wandered into the middle of Palermo. Its front is so strongly patterned that even a quick snap looks good.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Marina, across the square from the main facade, on the side facing the palace. The palace lies to the east of you, so face east and let the open square frame it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole facade in. Then try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the windows and the crenellated top. Use zoom 0.5x only if you're close to the walls, and keep your phone level so the lines don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade's vertical edges with them so the walls stand up straight.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or later in the afternoon, when the sun is lower and the stonework gets soft shadows. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try Piazza Marina, on the square with the palace facade behind you as you face the square's open side. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit low so the palace sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square, on the side facing the palace, while you stand in front of the facade on the Piazza Marina side, so the whole building fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: If you go inside, photos are generally fine for personal use, but flash is usually not allowed. It's a working university building, so check the official site before you visit.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one close-up of the paired windows with a tiny passer-by in the corner to show how huge those walls are.
card.good_to_know: Palazzo Chiaramonte, also called Lo Steri, was begun by 1320 for the powerful Sicilian lord Manfredi III Chiaramonte. Later it housed the Spanish viceroys and the Royal Customs, and from 1600 to 1782 it was the seat of the Inquisition's tribunal. Today it's a museum and also holds the University of Palermo's rector's offices.

card.hook: Stand on Piazza Bellini and you get the Palermo postcard in one go: a calm, pale church front with two older churches standing either side of it like bookends.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Bellini, on the square facing the main façade, with the church's north side in front of you. You should see the double-ramp staircase and the late Renaissance portal, with the Martorana and San Cataldo churches across the square.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so you get the whole façade and its neighbours. Use 0.5x only if you can't step back far enough, and 2x or more for the portal and the staircase.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines to keep the stair ramps and the cornice straight, then tap the pale stone of the façade and slide a touch darker so the sky stays blue.

card.challenge: Take a shot where the Martorana and San Cataldo are both in the frame, and the staircase is perfectly straight. Bonus point if nobody walks through it.
card.good_to_know: A will of 1310 paid for a women's Dominican convent here, on the site of an admiral's palace. The church was enlarged mainly between 1566 and 1596 and inaugurated on 24 November 1596. Its dome was finished in 1750.

card.hook: Picture a palace from the 1100s with thick walls and tiny windows, built to keep summer heat out. Today it's a tall, calm, perfectly symmetrical facade with a ribbon of water running straight to the door.
card.stand_here: Stand in the Giardino della Zisa, the front garden facing the main facade. Face west and you'll see the facade with the central water axis and the garden planting framing it in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole facade with the garden in front. If you're too close to fit it all, tap 0.5x. For details like the entrance or the top of the walls, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water axis on the centre line and keep your phone level, so the palace sits straight at the end of it.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon light is kinder to stone than harsh midday sun. One page suggests the facade looks best in the afternoon, around 3 to 5 PM.
card.selfie_here: Head to Piazza della Zisa, with the palace silhouette behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if it's available, and keep the palace over your shoulder. The open ground in front of the facade also works as a backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Piazza della Zisa, stepping back far enough to take in the whole palace, while you stand in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: The garden is reported to be open without a ticket, but the palace interior is separate and may be closed at times, so check the official site first. Some industrial areas near the Zisa are best visited in daytime and in a group.
card.challenge: Can you get a shot where the water axis points at the door like an arrow, and your shadow is the only thing out of line?
card.good_to_know: Work began around 1165 under King William I, using Arab craftsmen, and finished in 1189 under William II. The name comes from an Arabic word meaning 'the Dear one' or 'the Splendid one'. It was once part of a much larger royal hunting park, though the gardens are long gone. In 2015 it joined the UNESCO Arab-Norman Palermo World Heritage Site.

card.hook: The front of the Gesù is the calm, well-behaved bit of a church that goes completely wild inside. Outside, it's all tidy lines and neat rows of statues, which makes it a great clean shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Casa Professa, right in front of the main façade. From here the church is to the south-east, so face that way and take in the whole front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade in from the square, then try 1x for a more natural look. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the statues in the niches and the portals.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up one vertical edge of the façade with a grid line, so the tall building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Check how the light falls on the stonework when you arrive. Going early in the day is a good bet if you want a quieter square.
card.selfie_here: Climb the steps below the façade, turn your back to the church and face out into the piazza. Use the front camera at 0.5x and the façade will sit nicely over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a place of worship, so dress respectfully if you go inside. Check the official site before you go for visiting times and any photography rules.
card.challenge: Find all three statues in the niches above the portals (St Ignatius of Loyola, a Madonna with Child and Francis Xavier) and get each one in its own zoomed shot.
card.good_to_know: The Church of the Gesù is also called Casa Professa. The Jesuits arrived in Palermo in 1549, and the dome was finished in 1686. A bomb brought the dome down in 1943, and after a long restoration the church reopened on 24 February 2009.

card.hook: Those red domes look like they've been glowing since the Middle Ages, but the bright red is a 19th-century paint job. It's still the first thing everyone wants on their phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Largo Michele Gerbasi and face the church so all five red domes sit in one frame. Check the square on the map first, then shuffle around until you find a clear line of sight.
card.zoom: Start at 1x and leave a little empty sky above the domes so they don't feel cramped. If they look small and far away, tap 2x to fill the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the domes up with a horizontal grid line, then tap a dome and slide the brightness down a touch so the red stays rich and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder to the red domes than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Inside the cloister garden, stand between the twin columns with the small domes of the church over your shoulder, and use the front camera. You can also try the monastery garden footbridge, where a reviewer says you get a good view of the red domes behind you.
card.ask_someone: Stay in Largo Michele Gerbasi with your back to the church and ask a passer-by to step back and frame you with the whole church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The cloister and church site may be ticketed or have set opening times, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with all five domes, then one close shot with the small domes peeking over the ruined cloister arches and the citrus trees.
card.good_to_know: A church and Benedictine monastery stood here before the 6th century. Around 1136, after the Norman conquest, Roger II of Sicily gave it back to Benedictine monks. The domes show the Arab influence that lingered in Sicily when the church was rebuilt in the 12th century, and the red was added in the 19th century after traces of red plaster were found.

card.hook: Three bright red domes sit on top of a plain pale stone block, and somehow it's the most photogenic roof in Palermo. Against a blue sky, they look almost cartoon-bright.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza Bellini, in front of the church, and face the facade. The church is just to the south of this point, so you'll see the facade and bell tower with the red domes above, and the Martorana church right beside it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the facade, bell tower and domes in from close range. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the red domes against the sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the bell tower upright, then tap the stonework and drag the brightness down a little so the red domes and the sky keep their colour.
card.best_time: Go in the warm light of late afternoon, at golden hour. The pale stone glows and the red domes look richer.
card.selfie_here: Take it in Piazza Bellini, in the square beside the church. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and tuck the three red domes in behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the square directly in front of the church, so the whole facade and domes fit in the frame, while you stand a little closer to the church.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is generally allowed inside the church, but skip the flash, especially during services or quiet moments. It's a place of worship, so opening times may vary. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get all three domes in one shot with the Martorana church peeking in at the edge, then step closer and fill the frame with red.
card.good_to_know: San Cataldo dates from the mid-12th century and is built in the Arab-Norman style, which is found only in Sicily. In the 18th century it was used as a post office, and it joined the World Heritage list in 2015. Inside, the original mosaic floor survives, and part of the old city wall runs underneath.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza Bellini, in front of the church, and face the facade. The church is just to the south of this point, so you'll see the facade and bell tower with the red domes above, and the Martorana church right beside it.

card.hook: Picture a lake lapping at these walls, with royal evening parties going on inside. The lake is long gone, so the Cuba now stands up tall and a bit surprised in the middle of Palermo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Corso Calatafimi and face the front of the palace, with its big blind pointed arches. There's no single perfect spot, so shuffle along the pavement until nothing blocks the facade, then step back as far as is safe.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole building in. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, try zoom 0.5x. Then go to zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the arches and the Arabic lettering along the top.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the corners of the building with the vertical lines so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer, warmer light on the sandy stone. Midday sun is harsh and flattens the arches.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, hold it a little low and switch to 0.5x if your phone has it. Turn so the palace sits over your shoulder, and tilt the phone up so the arches stay in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Watch the traffic when you step back from the kerb. Personal photos are allowed inside without flash, but professional photography needs prior permission. The courtyard is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one straight-on shot with the walls dead vertical, then one from a slight angle. Which one shows off the tower-like middle section better?
card.good_to_know: The Cuba was built in 1180 for William II of Sicily as a cool retreat for hot days and evening parties. The name probably comes from its cube shape, or from the Arabic word for dome. Boccaccio even set one of his Decameron tales here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Corso Calatafimi and face the front of the palace, with its big blind pointed arches. There's no single perfect spot, so shuffle along the pavement until nothing blocks the facade, then step back as far as is safe.

card.hook: Imagine a quiet street in Palermo's Kalsa quarter, then a door that opens onto a hall full of white stucco figures acting out the life of St Francis. It's a lovely surprise, and your phone will enjoy it.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, in the Kalsa quarter right by the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi. For the outside, step back on the street and face the building. Inside, stand near the entrance and face the room so you can see the whole wall.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the building and the whole room. Try zoom 0.5x if the space feels tight and you want the whole wall in. Then go to zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single stucco figures without leaning in.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the scene, then drag the slider to make it a little darker so the stucco keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Check the official site for visiting times, then pick the quietest slot you can. You'll get a cleaner view of the room with fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to fit more in, and hold the phone a little higher. Turn so the oratory or the nearby basilica sits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside are generally allowed, but never with flash, as it can harm the artworks. Rules and entry arrangements can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole wall, then find your favourite stucco figure and make it the star of a close-up.
card.good_to_know: The oratory was built in 1569 and paid for by a confraternity of mainly Genoese merchants. Giacomo Serpotta added the stucco decoration between 1699 and 1706. Caravaggio's Nativity with St Francis and St Lawrence was stolen in 1969 and never recovered, so since 2015 a hi-tech replica hangs in its place.
